why: R7.4's LEDGER ROW, and the first case in this package to carry clock facts. alice invited bob at t=0 and his invitation expires at 30000000000ns -- which is what the expiry observation answers. The run's clock then moved to 30000000001, ONE TICK past it, and bob's `event.joined` claim was made there: the application honored an invitation after it had stopped being honorable. `honored_past_expiry` reads the join's own `t` against the observation's value, and `finding` falls to its default `bug`. THE TIME OF THE JOIN AND NOT THE TIME OF THE CHECK is the whole of the rule: `input.clock.now` is the same number here either way, so a rule reading it could not tell this case from an honest one whose clock advanced afterwards. EVERY CLAIM CARRIES ITS `t` HERE, which tests/engine's two-path arm is what taught me: the LEDGER path derives the time from the clock facts and the CASE path reads this block, so a hand-written claim with no `t` made the two disagree about which case kills a mutant -- the ledger said the row fires and the case said it does not.
